text:
Africa’s clean-cooking acceleration has a paradox at its centre: the fuel delivering the fastest gains is also creating the largest common exposure.

LPG now provides more than 70% of Africa’s clean-cooking access. It is familiar, controllable, fast and capable of handling the meals households actually cook. In cities where charcoal is expensive and electricity unreliable, it can be the most practical route away from smoke.

The progress is real. Almost US$740 million of the US$2.2 billion pledged at the 2024 Summit on Clean Cooking in Africa had been disbursed by the end of May 2026. Nearly 12 million people in sub-Saharan Africa gained access in 2024 — three times the annual gain recorded in 2010.

But population growth still outpaced new access. Roughly 970 million people in sub-Saharan Africa remain without clean cooking.

And the 2026 disruption around the Strait of Hormuz exposed the vulnerability behind LPG’s success. The IEA estimates that around 30% of global seaborne LPG trade passes through the strait. Physical shortages were limited in Africa, but prices rose sharply in some markets. Many emerging economies held less than 30 days of LPG demand in operational and strategic storage.

StoneComms’ conclusion is not that Africa should retreat from LPG. It is that clean-cooking policy should stop treating first adoption as the end of the problem.

Households already behave like energy portfolio managers. A 2026 Clean Cooking Alliance study across seven companies found customers typically used two or three fuels, with the promoted technology handling around half of cooking tasks. Cost matters, but so do burner count, long boiling, cookware, outages, fuel availability and whether a supplier survives.

Kenya’s KOKO Networks closure made that last risk tangible: a large installed base of ethanol stoves was left without its intended fuel network.

StoneComms proposes a resilience-adjusted clean-cooking test built around six questions:

How much polluting cooking is actually displaced?
Can users keep affording the fuel?
What happens when supply or a provider fails?
Does the technology fit real meals?
How much durable local value is created?
Can households switch between clean options without falling back into smoke?

The policy objective should be clean optionality, not permanent dependence on polluting fallback.

For governments, DFIs, investors and manufacturers, the useful question is no longer simply “how many stoves were distributed?” It is: how many meals stay clean after the next price shock, outage or provider failure?
